notes.meaning: Moses finished setting up the tabernacle and poured holy oil on it to set it apart for God. Consecrated means made holy and devoted entirely to the Lord's service. The phrase about the day points to the general time when the sacred tent was fully assembled and ready for worship.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that taken literally, the date given here is a month earlier than the census in chapter 1, suggesting the phrase refers loosely to the general period after the tabernacle was built.

notes.meaning: The leaders of the twelve tribes brought six covered wagons and twelve oxen as a joint gift. Two leaders shared the cost of each wagon, and each leader gave one ox to pull them. Even though God had not directly commanded wagons, these rulers took the lead to provide safe transport for the sacred tent.

The Lord told Moses to accept these wagons and oxen for the work of the tabernacle. They were to be distributed among the Levites according to the specific job each group had to do. Those who lead in wealth and rank showed a godly example by freely supporting the Lord's house.
Moses obeyed the Lord and handed the wagons and oxen over to the Levites. This showed that God welcomed their voluntary gifts to help his servants do their work.

Moses gave two wagons and four oxen to the family of Gershon, who carried the curtains and cloth hangings. He gave four wagons and eight oxen to the family of Merari, because they had to move the heavy wooden frames, posts, and metal bases. God wisely gave more help to the workers who had the heaviest load to bear.

The family of Kohath received no wagons because their task was to carry the most sacred furnishings on their shoulders using poles. God required these holy objects to be carried with special reverence rather than pulled by animals. When people later tried to move the ark on a cart in King David's day, it led to tragedy because they did not follow this rule.

The tribal leaders came forward to dedicate the altar with their gifts once it had been anointed with oil. God told Moses to have only one leader present his offering each day over twelve days. Spreading the gifts out ensured that each tribe was honored equally and the sacrifices could be handled in an orderly way.

Nahshon from the tribe of Judah was the first leader to bring his offering. Judah had been given the lead position in the camp layout, honoring the ancient promise that a ruler would come from this tribe. Nahshon presented these expensive gifts on behalf of all the people in his tribe.

Nahshon brought a large silver dish and a silver bowl, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering, along with a gold saucer holding sweet-smelling incense. The silver vessels were used in the outer courtyard around the bronze altar, while the gold saucer was meant for the altar of incense. These costly dishes showed that the people wanted to honor the Lord with their very best goods.

Nahshon also brought animals for three kinds of sacrifices: burnt offerings of total dedication, a goat for a sin offering to ask for forgiveness, and peace offerings. Peace offerings were shared meals where the priests, the leaders, and worshippers feasted together in thankful fellowship with God. Even in the midst of joyful celebration, the sin offering reminded them that human beings always need God's mercy.

Nethanel, the leader of the tribe of Issachar, brought his offering on the second day. Issachar encamped right next to Judah, so their leader stepped forward next in line according to God's orderly camp plan.

Nethanel presented the exact same metal dishes and grain offerings as Nahshon had on day one. His tribe gave a heavy silver dish, a silver bowl of fine flour with oil, and a golden dish filled with incense. Bringing matching gifts showed that every tribe shared an equal role in worship and held the same standing before God.

Nethanel brought the required sacrificial animals: a bull, a ram, and a lamb for a burnt offering, a goat for a sin offering, and twenty-one animals for peace offerings. These animals were offered immediately on the altar, allowing the community to celebrate with a holy feast of thanksgiving. Each tribe had an equal stake in the altar of the Lord.
On the third day, Eliab, the leader of Zebulun, came forward to dedicate the altar. Zebulun was the third tribe positioned on the east side of the tabernacle under Judah's standard.

Eliab presented a silver platter, a silver bowl filled with flour and oil, and a golden incense dish. The Bible records the full list for every tribe individually to show that God values each tribe's gift and forgets none of them.

Eliab completed his tribe's dedication by presenting animals for a burnt offering, a sin offering, and peace offerings. The peace offering provided a sacred meal of fellowship between God and his people. Repeating this service day by day allowed the priests to carry out the sacrifices carefully and without excess.

On the fourth day, Elizur, the leader of the tribe of Reuben, came near with his offering. Reuben was Jacob's firstborn son, but in the camp arrangement his division marched second, right after the camp of Judah.
